catalog_quote: It is well-known that stress in Chinese is hard to feel. ... Chao (1968: 35) suggests that in a string of full syllables, the last has most stress, the first has slightly less, and the rest have still less. This is known as the ‘medium-light-heavy’ theory. However, as Chao (1968: 38) acknowledges, Mandarin speakers do not agree on where stress is, therefore the medium-light-heavy theory is hard to confirm. ... In dialects like Mandarin, there is a difference between full syllables, such as le4 ‘happy,’ and weak syllables, such as the aspect marker le (which indicates completion). Full syllables are longer and carry tone. Weak syllables are shorter and usually do not carry tone. Intuitively, full syllables have more stress than weak syllables. ... If we exclude contrastive stress and weak syllables, then it is quite true to say that native speakers can hardly feel stress in Chinese. ... …
sweep_summary: Mandarin (mand1415) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Duanmu 2000/2011 (open-text grade). Of the 18 title-sweep items, none is a first-hand word-stress description that could be read: the only candidates are Shen 1990 'The Prosody of Mandarin Chinese' (UC Press, print-only: no ebook, not in HathiTrust, PDF of the companion Shen 1986 CLAO article sits behind Persée's altcha) and, less likely, Shen 1991 and Shih 1997 on T3 sandhi (paywalled) and Li Kening 2009 (not located). Four items were fetched sources and read in full (Ou 2019, Wang et al. 2020, Arcodia & Montermini 2012 — all silent on Mandarin word stress) plus Yang et al. 2019's abstract; the rest are intonation, discourse, L2 or non-linguistic 'accent' items, or the wrong variety (Chengdu). The best new first-hand statement came from a source already on file: Duanmu's 1990 MIT dissertation, sec. 5.1 p. 181 and rule (8) p. 184, which confirms the lexical coding (neutral-tone syllables lexically marked; all regular syllables stressed; relative prominence unclear, Hoa 1983 vs Meredith 1990) but does not supersede Duanmu 2000/2011. An open 2024 Language and Cognition paper (Yu et al.) adds the Chinese-side citations on the disputed Strong-Weak vs Weak-Strong patterns. Tool budgets (web lookups, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex) ran out mid-sweep; Cloudflare blocked Benjamins, T&F, AIP, Persée PDF, MUSE and Duanmu's UMich pages. All fetched sources files and API records are under with.

new_statements.quote: Mandarin has two kinds of syllables, stressed and unstressed. Unstressed syllables, also called 'neutral-tone syllables', are toneless and monomoraic, and are mostly marked lexically (Woo 1969, C.Cheng 1973, Chao 1968, H. Lin & Yan 1988). In contrast, stressed syllables, which comprise the overwhelming majority, always have tones and are bimoraic (or sometimes trimoraic finally) in length (cf. Chapter 2). [fn. 1] Among stressed syllables, some may bear greater stress than others. Hoa (1983) suggests that such additional stress is at least partly marked in the lexicon, while Meredith (1990) suggests that it is predictable from the tones of the syllables. My own experience with native Peking Mandarin speakers suggests that while there is never confusion between stressed and unstressed syllables, judgements on the relative prominence of stressed syllables are less clear.
new_statements.citation: Duanmu, San (1990). A Formal Study of Syllable, Tone, Stress and Domain in Chinese Languages. PhD dissertation, MIT.
new_statements.locator: sec. 5.1 'Mandarin', p. 181 (body and fn. 1); stress rules (8) p. 184
new_statements.reading: First-hand, by the same author as the catalog's deciding source but ten years earlier: the stressed/unstressed split coincides with full-tone vs neutral-tone syllables and is a lexical property of the morpheme ('mostly marked lexically'); every regular syllable is stressed (rule (8a) 'Mark all regular syllables', p. 184) and stress domains are left-headed; relative prominence among full syllables is not reliably perceived and is contested (Hoa lexical vs Meredith tone-predictable). This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' kind and its prule/srule wording.

sources.quote: In addition, Mandarin has a neutral tone that signals an unstressed syllable and always occurs in the final syllable of a word. ... Mandarin disyllabic words have two stress patterns, namely, the Strong-Weak and the Weak-Strong pattern (Lu, 1984; Yin, 1982). ... Some researchers believe that both Strong-Weak and Weak-Strong patterns are equally common in Mandarin, while others argued that the Strong-Weak pattern is predominant (Wang & Feng, 2006). There are also researchers considering that the Weak-Strong pattern is the principal pattern (Lin et al., 1984; Xu, 1982), although it is argued that there is no fixed stress pattern in Mandarin (Liu, 2007; Zhou, 2018).
sources.note: OA full text read (Introduction). Second-hand summary of the Chinese-language literature: neutral tone marks an unstressed syllable and 'always occurs in the final syllable of a word'; among full-toned disyllables there are Strong-Weak and Weak-Strong patterns and the literature is contradictory on which predominates (Wang & Feng 2006: SW; Lin, Yan & Sun 1984, Xu 1982: WS; Liu 2007, Zhou 2018: no fixed pattern). Refines the catalog's 'disputed relative prominence' note with the Chinese-side citations; consistent with lexical coding.
